headline: Nomimono is 飲み (nomi, the stem of the verb 飲む) plus 物 (-mono, “thing”).
Otona appears in sources from the Heian period, from Old Japanese.
Tokidoki is a reduplication of 時 (toki, “time”), with rendaku.
Tomaru is inherited from Old Japanese, and a doublet of 泊まる (tomaru).
Atsui for hot objects is cognate with 暑い, the one used for hot weather.
Minasan is 皆 (mina, “everybody, everyone”) plus さん (-san), used when addressing a group.
Tsuyoi is found in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, from Proto-Japonic *tuyə.
Ashi was asi in Old Japanese, and may be related to an older a for “leg; foot”.
Ichiban is simply 一 (ichi) plus 番 (-ban).
Au has no settled origin: one theory has it imitating the sound of the upper and lower lips meeting.
Naku is a verbalization of na-, the bound form of 音 (ne, “sound, voice”), and a doublet of 泣く (naku, “to cry”).
Sugiru is likely cognate with 直ぐ (sugu, “straight; soon”), and first attested in the Kojiki of 712.
Minami is Old Japanese 南 (mi1nami1).
Chikai is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *tika.
Tariru is an irregular conjugation shift from 足る (taru), which was originally quadrigrade.
Reizōko is 冷蔵 (reizō, “refrigeration”) plus 庫 (-ko, “depository”).
Narau is related to 倣う (narau, “to imitate”).
Natsu was natu: from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *natu.
Asobu is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, from Proto-Japonic *asonpu.
Kekkō is from Middle Chinese 結構, appearing in the diary of Fujiwara no Sanesuke in 1031.
Aruku is Old Japanese, first cited to the Man'yōshū of circa 759 CE.
Asa is attested in the Man'yōshū of 759, and its old day cycle began in the afternoon.
Shiru is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *siru.
Miseru is from Old Japanese 見す (misu), a lower bigrade verb.
Iru “to need” is the same word as 入る (iru, “to enter”).
Hataraku is most likely derived from a mimetic word はた (hata), perhaps the sound of objects bumping together.
Futoi was 太し (puto1si) in Old Japanese.
Kakeru comes from Old Japanese 掛く (kaku), a lower bigrade verb.
Tōi is from Proto-Japonic *təpə, with cognates in Miyako and Okinawan.
Osara is 御 (o-, polite prefix) plus 皿 (sara, “plate”).
Kimeru is the transitive form of Old Japanese 決む (kimu), a verb that can be either transitive or intransitive.
